name: Violet Purple
lede: Violet Purple is a dark blue-violet from the color list Patrick Syme published in 1814 for naturalists, named by pushing Werner's older violet blue toward purple.

sections.title: A name from a nomenclature
sections.body:
Violet purple is not a flower's name or a dye's. It is a term from a color list made for naturalists, which makes it unusual among the names in our archive [1][2]. Abraham Gottlob Werner, the mineralogist at Freiberg, drew up a short list of colors for describing minerals; his student Robert Jameson published an English version in 1805 [1]. In 1814 the Scottish flower painter Patrick Syme expanded the list to 108 terms, added a painted swatch for each, and in 1821 raised it to 110 [1].

Syme made purple and orange principal colors, which forced renaming. Werner's *violet blue* became violet purple, and *plum blue* became plum purple [1][2]. Syme's own contribution was to fill the group with flower names such as [[pansy-purple]] and [[auricula-purple]] [2]. Next to it in his list sat [[campanula-purple]], and the whole family reads as blues taken toward red [3][2].

sections.title: What the swatch is
sections.body:
The swatch here, a dark blue-violet, comes from Werner's list as printed in 1821, where violet purple is number 37 in the purples [4]. It is an aged plate, so treat the exact value as approximate [4]. Our library also places it in ISCC-NBS block 238, a dark purple, with a measured difference of about 6 on the CIEDE2000 scale [4].

The name has not stayed with one color. Ridgway's 1912 *Color Standards*, plate XI, uses the same words for a much brighter, magenta-leaning purple, far from Syme's dark one [4]. That is the usual trap with historical names: the words survive and the paint changes. If you meet "violet purple" in a text, check whose list it comes from before picturing a color. Plainer [[purple]] is the safe parent term.

sections.title: Syme's examples
sections.body:
Syme anchored each color to things you could go and look at. For violet purple he named the purple aster among plants and [[gem:amethyst|amethyst]] among minerals [3]. The animal example was the wing feathers of the male steel-backed flycatcher, drawn by John Gould in his work on New Guinea (1875-88) [3]. For mixing, the recipe was Berlin blue with red and a little brown [3]. His nearby pansy purple was indigo with carmine and a touch of black, which shows how dark these purples were meant to be [3].

The name outlived him. A French catalogue of 1905, Dauthenay and Oberthür's *Répertoire de couleurs*, used violet purple, primrose yellow and China blue, though its authors do not seem to have consulted Syme [5]. Baty takes this as a sign of how deeply his names had entered botanical vocabulary [5].

sections.title: Not Pliny's violet purple
sections.body: A different "violet purple" appears in translations of Pliny, who quotes an older writer on shellfish dyes [6]. In that passage the violet purple cost 100 denarii a pound, then came Tarentine red, and last the Tyrian dye at more than 1,000 denarii a pound [6]. That is a murex dye fashion from the speaker's youth, and it has no connection to Syme's aster-and-amethyst swatch [6]. The two share only an English phrase [6].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
As a painted color this deep violet is uncommon. In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of this swatch covers at least five per cent of the canvas in 30 of them [7]. Where it appears, it mostly plays the role of a shadow tone, 87 per cent of the time, rather than a midtone [7]. The largest share is in Bronzino's *Portrait of a girl* (about 1545), where it covers 40 per cent of the picture [7].

The color is far more common in the 1900s, with 10 of 1,674 paintings against 7 of 8,345 in the 1800s, a lift of about 4.7 [7]. The earliest match is Ambrogio Lorenzetti's *Presentation at the Temple* (1342), where it covers about six per cent [7]. As always these are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, and a color match is not a pigment test [7]. A museum visitor can use the idea anyway: look for the near-black purple in a velvet sleeve or a shadowed robe.

openers: Violet Purple was invented for describing minerals and flowers, not for dyers or painters.
The same two words name a dark violet in 1821 and a bright magenta-leaning purple in 1912.
